Fly
flī
n. and v. (a winged insect, sent as a plague and used as a figure of small corruption; also to move on wings)
Old English fleoge, an insect, and fleogan, to move through the air. The Hebrew arob of the fourth plague is a swarm; zebub is the common fly, and gives the name Baalzebub, lord of the flies.

Biblical Definition

The fourth plague on Egypt: “Else, if thou wilt not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies upon thee, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people, and into thy houses” (Exo 8:21); and it came — “there came a grievous swarm of flies into the house of Pharaoh, and into his servants' houses, and into all the land of Egypt: the land was corrupted by reason of the swarm of flies” (Exo 8:24). The psalmist sets it in one line of a history: “He spake, and there came divers sorts of flies, and lice in all their coasts” (Psa 105:31) — he spake, and an empire was undone by insects. Isaiah makes the fly an instrument of summons: “the LORD shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria” (Isa 7:18), armies called like insects with a whistle. And Ecclesiastes gives the proverb that has outlived the plague: “Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour” (Ecc 10:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a fly as a winged insect of various species, and to fly as to move through air by the aid of wings; also to move swiftly, or to flee.

expand to see more

FLY, v.i. To move through air by the aid of wings, as fowls.

2. To move or pass with velocity or celerity.

3. To flee; to run away; to attempt to escape.

FLY, n. A winged insect of numerous species. Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour. Eccl. x.

Key Scripture

Exo 8:21 — "Else, if thou wilt not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies upon thee, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people, and into thy houses: and the houses of the Egyptians shall be full of swarms of flies, and also the ground whereon they are."

Exo 8:24 — "And the LORD did so; and there came a grievous swarm of flies into the house of Pharaoh, and into his servants' houses, and into all the land of Egypt: the land was corrupted by reason of the swarm of flies."

Ecc 10:1 — "Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour."

Isa 7:18 — "And it shall come to pass in that day, that the LORD shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria."

Modern Corruption

A long-built reputation is thought to absorb a small folly, and Ecclesiastes says the small folly is exactly what ruins the whole jar.

expand to see more

The Preacher's figure is a pot of costly ointment — the apothecary's work, compounded with care and worth a great deal — and two dead flies in it. The ointment is not diluted; it is spoiled, and what comes out of the jar now is a stinking savour. He then names the application without softening it: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour. The modern instinct is to weigh a man's failures against his contribution and conclude that the ledger still favours him, and there is a place for that charity; Scripture does not erase David for Bathsheba or Peter for the courtyard. But the proverb is about savour rather than accounting. A little folly in a man of standing changes what people smell when the jar is opened, and no quantity of former excellence puts the flies back out.

The plague half of the word carries a different warning. Egypt's gods included flies and beetles, and Ekron worshipped Baalzebub, the lord of the flies, whose name the Jews later used for the prince of the devils. God's judgment on Egypt came through the creatures Egypt revered — the Nile turned, the frogs, the flies, the cattle, the sun darkened — so that each plague dismantled a deity. And Psalm 105 gives the whole account in three words: he spake. Isaiah's image extends it to nations: the LORD hisses, as a beekeeper whistles his swarm, and Egypt and Assyria come. Empires that never heard of Him move at a signal. That is the doctrine of providence over the nations, and it is why the church may be sober about world events without being frightened by them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew arob (H6157), a swarm of flies, of the fourth plague; zebub (H2070), a fly, and the element in Baalzebub; Greek Beelzeboul (G954), the prince of the devils.

expand to see more

Hebrew arob (H6157) — a mixture, a swarm; swarms of flies upon Pharaoh and his houses; Exodus 8:21.

Hebrew zebub (H2070) — a fly; dead flies in the apothecary's ointment; Ecclesiastes 10:1.

Hebrew Baal zebub — lord of the fly; the god of Ekron whom Ahaziah consulted; 2 Kings 1:2.

Hebrew sharaq (H8319) — to hiss, to whistle; the LORD shall hiss for the fly; Isaiah 7:18.

Greek Beelzeboul (G954) — Beelzebub, the prince of the devils in the Gospels; Matthew 12:24.

Usage

"“The land was corrupted by reason of the swarm of flies” — an empire undone by insects."

"“He spake, and there came divers sorts of flies” — the whole account in three words."

"“Dead flies cause the ointment… to send forth a stinking savour” — a little folly in a man of reputation."
